script.opening: (Anxious, flustered, holding a notebook full of readings.) "Doctor, my home monitor is driving me mad — one minute it says 120-something, the next it's 178! I don't know what to believe or whether my tablets are working. I get myself in a state about it and then it goes up even more. Am I about to have a stroke? Should I be taking more tablets when it's high?"

facts.text: "Whenever I'm worried, I check. Then again if it's high. Sometimes straight after I've been rushing about." Sometimes over a cup of coffee, sometimes while talking on the phone. Uses either arm. Measures 6–8 times a day.
"I don't know about the cuff. I bought it online a while ago" — a wrist monitor, brand she doesn't recognise. Arm circumference: she's a size 18.

"Not that I've noticed." If asked specifically about standing up: "Now you say it, I do go light-headed getting out of bed sometimes" — the low readings were usually in the morning. No falls or faints.
"I'm not sure — I've not really paid attention." If asked to feel it on camera: seems regular to her. No palpitations.

"I take it every day, I don't think I've missed any" — amlodipine 10 mg in the morning (increased 2 months ago from 5 mg). Ankles a bit puffy since. No other medicines; no NSAIDs or decongestants. No allergies.
"No, just the panic" — no headaches, chest pain, visual problems or weakness.
Hypertension for 4 years. Type 2 diabetes? No. Kidneys fine at last bloods. Retired school cook, widowed, lives alone. Her friend had a stroke last year. Non-smoker, rarely drinks.

Anxious: "Every time I see a big number I think, this is it." Wants clarity: "Tell me which numbers to believe, and whether I need more tablets." Relieved by a clear routine: "So the 178 isn't real?" Surprised: "I hadn't thought about the low ones." Asks: "Even if I feel funny?" If told to take an extra tablet when high, she would (the trap).

ice.ideas: "My blood pressure is all over the place and the tablets aren't working."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of a stroke like her friend's; the checking and worry feed each other; she lives alone and feels nobody to ask.
ice.expectations: "Which numbers to believe — and whether to take more tablets when it's high."

cues: "Whenever I'm worried, I check." — technique and anxiety.
"Am I about to have a stroke?" — the fear to address.
"Light-headed getting out of bed." — postural drop, if asked.

checkpoints.text: Interprets variable readings SYSTEMATICALLY rather than reacting to the highest number — explicitly does NOT advise reactive extra dosing for single high readings

Assesses TECHNIQUE/confounders — validated/calibrated machine, correct cuff size, a few minutes’ seated rest, arm supported at heart level, not talking, no caffeine/smoking/exercise/full bladder, two readings a minute apart twice daily for 4–7 days with the first day discarded and the rest averaged (NICE NG136), consistent timing, higher-reading arm if the difference is over 15 mmHg
Recognises WHITE-COAT/situational rises and the ANXIETY cycle (worry raises readings), addressing the anxiety as part of management without dismissing genuinely elevated averages

Screens POSTURAL HYPOTENSION (asks about dizziness/falls; standing BP checked face to face; NICE NG136 significant systolic fall ≥20 mmHg, with the diastolic ≥10 criterion from international consensus) given her symptoms and low readings on amlodipine — recognising the low readings/over-treatment may matter as much as the high ones

Considers ARRHYTHMIA/irregular pulse (AF makes oscillometric monitors unreliable — palpate the pulse face to face, measure BP manually if irregular, ECG) and other causes (adherence, pain, device error), then STANDARDISES with correct home monitoring and ABPM/standardised clinic readings before changing treatment

Reassures with a clear systematic explanation (variability is usually technique/physiology, not impending stroke), calming the anxiety that is itself raising readings, without dismissing real findings
Gives a clear, confidence-restoring correct-monitoring routine and checks understanding (teach-back of technique)

Safety-nets and follows up: ABPM/standardised readings and pulse/ECG check, review of medication on reliable data, postural-symptom and arrhythmia red flags, anxiety support, and when to seek urgent help (very high BP with symptoms) — systematic interpretation, not reactive dosing

worked.txt: "First, take a breath — you are not about to have a stroke, and please don’t take extra tablets when a reading’s high; that can do harm. Wildly different numbers almost always mean something about how the readings are being taken, not that your pressure is dangerously swinging. Let’s work out why."

"Tell me how you measure it … A few things matter a lot: sit quietly and rest for a few minutes first, arm resting on a table level with your heart, feet flat, don’t talk, no coffee or rushing beforehand, and take two readings a minute apart, morning and evening for a week — we leave out the first day and use the average, not the one scary reading. Same arm each time."

"You’ve spotted it yourself — you get in a state and it goes up. That’s real: worry pushes the reading up, which makes you worry more. Settling that loop is part of the treatment, not separate from it."

"Two things I want to check properly when you come in to see the nurse, as I can’t do them over video: your blood pressure sitting and then standing, because the tablet you’re on can make it drop when you stand — those low readings matter — and your pulse, because an irregular heartbeat can make home monitors give crazy numbers — if it is irregular she’ll measure it by hand and we’ll do a heart tracing."
"To really know your blood pressure, let’s use a 24-hour monitor or a proper week of correctly-taken home readings. Then we judge your tablets on solid information, not on the alarming odd reading."

"If you ever get a very high reading WITH symptoms — bad headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision or speech changes — that’s urgent, seek help. Otherwise, do the readings the way we’ve agreed and we’ll review with the monitor results. You’ll feel much more in control once the numbers are reliable."

f.learning: Wildly variable home BP readings should be interpreted SYSTEMATICALLY, not reacted to by chasing the highest number or dosing reactively (which is unsafe and anxiety-driven). Most variability is a MEASUREMENT/technique or physiological issue: check a validated, calibrated machine and correct CUFF SIZE (too-small over-reads), ensure the patient is seated, relaxed and rested for a few minutes with the arm supported at HEART LEVEL, feet flat, not talking, with no caffeine/smoking/exercise/full bladder beforehand, follows the NICE NG136 home protocol — two readings at least a minute apart, morning and evening, for at least 4 and ideally 7 days, DISCARDING THE FIRST DAY and AVERAGING the rest — measures at a consistent time, and uses the higher-reading arm if the two arms differ by more than 15 mmHg on repeat — correcting these often resolves the "wild" swings. Recognise WHITE-COAT and situational rises and the ANXIETY cycle (worry raises readings, which raises worry), and treat the anxiety as part of management without dismissing genuinely elevated averages. Importantly, ask about POSTURAL HYPOTENSION (NG136 checks standing BP in people with falls or postural dizziness, type 2 diabetes, or aged 80 and over; here her low readings on amlodipine justify a face-to-face check; a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant, and the diastolic ≥10 criterion is international consensus) — the low readings and possible over-treatment may matter as much as the high ones — and consider an IRREGULAR PULSE/ARRHYTHMIA such as atrial fibrillation, which makes oscillometric home monitors unreliable and erratic (palpate the pulse face to face, measure BP manually by auscultation if it is irregular, arrange an ECG per NICE NG196, and note AF changes overall management). Also consider adherence, pain and device error. Then STANDARDISE: teach correct home monitoring, arrange ABPM or properly standardised clinic/home readings to get a true picture, and review medication on reliable data. The hidden agenda is anxiety (fear of imminent stroke, temptation to over-dose) that itself raises readings — reassure with a clear systematic explanation, restore confidence with a correct-monitoring routine, screen the genuinely important things (postural drop, arrhythmia, true average), and review on reliable data, calming the anxiety while not missing real pathology.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults, updated 2026) · [2] NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation, 2021) · [3] British and Irish Hypertension Society, validated BP monitor list
knowledge.summary: Scattered home readings are a measurement problem until proven otherwise. Standardise technique, check the pulse for an irregular rhythm, look for a postural drop if she has symptoms, and judge treatment on a proper average — never on the highest single number.

points.t: NICE NG136 [1]: use validated, maintained and recalibrated devices (the BIHS list [3] helps patients choose); measure in a quiet, temperate setting, seated, relaxed, arm outstretched and supported, with the right cuff size. Measure both arms at first; if the difference is over 15 mmHg on repeat, use the arm with the higher reading.

NICE NG136 [1]: for each reading, two consecutive seated measurements at least 1 minute apart, twice daily (morning and evening), for at least 4 and ideally 7 days. Discard the first day’s measurements and average the rest. Random readings taken when anxious are not a valid average.

NICE NG136 [1]: palpate the pulse before automated measurement; if it is irregular, measure BP manually by auscultation, as automated devices may be inaccurate. An irregular pulse needs an ECG for atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196 [2]); AF also changes stroke-risk management.

NICE NG136 [1] (updated 2026): measure BP seated or lying, then after standing for at least 1 minute, in people with symptoms of postural hypotension (falls or postural dizziness), type 2 diabetes, or aged 80 and over. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant: review medicines, measure subsequent readings standing. (A diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more is part of the international consensus definition — international.)

NICE NG136 [1]: aged under 80, clinic below 140/90 and ABPM/HBPM below 135/85. Consider ABPM or HBPM alongside clinic readings where white-coat effect or masked hypertension is suspected. People who monitor at home should be given training and advice.
Amlodipine is long-acting (BNF); extra doses for a high reading do not act quickly and add to ankle swelling and postural symptoms. Change treatment only on a valid average.

NICE NG136 [1]: clinic BP ≥180/120 with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, AKI), needs same-day specialist referral. A single home 178/100 with no symptoms is not an emergency.
Worry and repeated checking raise readings. A fixed schedule, not checking when anxious, and addressing the health anxiety are part of management.

model.text: Hello Mrs Ferreira, I’m Dr Osei. Thank you for sending your readings. Before we look at them, tell me how this has been for you.
model.why: Starts with her experience, not the numbers

model.text: Doctor, it’s driving me mad. One minute 120-something, the next 178! I don’t know what to believe or whether my tablets work. I get in a state, and then it goes up more. Am I about to have a stroke? Should I take more tablets when it’s high?

model.why: Addresses the safety issue immediately and sets the agenda

model.text: Please. I just want to know what’s real.
Talk me through how you take a reading — when, where, and what you’re doing just before.
Whenever I’m worried, I check. Then again if it’s high. Sometimes straight after I’ve been rushing about.
That’s really helpful. And do you sit with your arm resting on a table? Do you know if the cuff is the right size for your arm, and whether the machine has been checked?
model.why: Checks posture, cuff size and device validation

model.text: I don’t know about the cuff. I bought it online a while ago.
We can check that. Do you ever notice your heart beating irregularly, fluttering or racing?
model.why: Screens for arrhythmia that makes automated readings unreliable

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed.
Do you ever feel dizzy or light-headed when you stand up, or have you had any falls?
I’m not sure — I’ve not really paid attention.
That’s fine, we can check it properly. How are you getting on with the amlodipine — any missed doses, ankle swelling?
I take it every day, I don’t think I’ve missed any.
And when you get a very high reading, have you had a severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, or any change in vision or speech?
model.why: Screens for symptoms that would make a reading urgent

model.text: No, just the panic.
You mentioned a stroke. Is that the main fear?
Yes. Every time I see a big number I think, this is it.
That sounds exhausting. What were you hoping I’d be able to do today?
Tell me which numbers to believe, and whether I need more tablets.

Here’s what I think is happening. Blood pressure changes minute to minute — with rushing, talking, worry, even a full bladder. When you check because you’re anxious, you catch it at its highest, and then the worry pushes it higher still. That’s a loop, not a stroke coming.
model.why: Explains variability and the anxiety cycle

model.text: So the 178 isn’t real?

It was real at that moment, but it isn’t your true average. We treat the average. There are two things I want to rule out: a heart rhythm that makes home machines give odd numbers, and blood pressure dropping when you stand, because the low readings matter too.
model.why: Frames AF and postural hypotension as the checks that matter

model.text: I hadn’t thought about the low ones.

So here’s a plan. Could you come in to see the nurse with your machine and cuff? She’ll check your pulse by hand, compare your machine with ours, measure your arm for the cuff, check both arms, and take your pressure sitting and then standing. If your pulse is irregular, we’ll do a heart tracing.
model.why: Face-to-face checks: device, cuff, pulse, both arms, postural BP, ECG if needed

model.text: Yes, I can do that.

Then a proper week of home readings. Morning and evening: sit for a few minutes, back supported, arm on a table at heart level, feet flat, no talking, no coffee or rushing just before. Take two readings a minute apart and write both down. Nothing in between — even if you feel worried.
Even if I feel funny?

If you feel unwell, that’s different — I’ll tell you exactly when to call. But checking because you’re anxious feeds the loop. We’ll average the week, leaving out the first day, and decide about your tablets on that. Can you tell me back how you’ll take them?
Twice a day, morning and night, sit first, arm on the table, two readings a minute apart, for a week. Not when I’m panicking.

Perfect. If you ever get a very high reading with a severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision or speech changes, or weakness on one side, call 999. If you feel faint or fall when standing, or notice your heart racing irregularly, ring us the same day. Otherwise I’ll see you with the week’s readings. Does that feel manageable?
model.why: Clear red flags, same-day triggers and follow-up

model.text: Much better. I feel like I know what I’m doing now.
You’ve done the right thing by asking. Reliable numbers will make this far less frightening.
model.why: Closes with reassurance tied to the plan

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you interpret data before acting on it. It is failed by chasing the highest number, by ignoring technique, and by brushing off the anxiety that drives the readings.

items.why: Changing treatment on unreliable readings is unsafe and may cause postural hypotension.
items.fix: Standardise first, then decide on the average.

items.fail: Never asking how she takes the readings.
items.why: Technique and timing explain most variability.
items.fix: Ask when, where and how; teach the NG136 HBPM routine.

items.fail: No pulse check or thought of AF.
items.why: NG136 requires a pulse check before automated measurement; AF makes readings erratic and changes management.
items.fix: Manual pulse, manual BP if irregular, ECG.

items.why: Low readings may reflect postural hypotension or over-treatment.
items.fix: Ask about postural symptoms; sitting and standing BP.

items.why: Dismissive labelling damages trust and misses the chance to break the loop.
items.fix: Explain how worry raises readings and agree a checking boundary.

items.why: Without it she will keep reacting to every number.
items.fix: Name the symptoms that need 999 or same-day contact; everything else waits for review.

NICE NG136 [1]: for each reading, two consecutive seated measurements at least 1 minute apart, twice daily (morning and evening), for at least 4 and ideally 7 days. Discard the first day’s measurements and average the rest. Random readings taken when anxious are not a valid average.

NICE NG136 [1]: palpate the pulse before automated measurement; if it is irregular, measure BP manually by auscultation, as automated devices may be inaccurate. An irregular pulse needs an ECG for atrial fibrillation (NICE NG196 [2]); AF also changes stroke-risk management.

NICE NG136 [1] (updated 2026): measure BP seated or lying, then after standing for at least 1 minute, in people with symptoms of postural hypotension (falls or postural dizziness), type 2 diabetes, or aged 80 and over. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant: review medicines, measure subsequent readings standing. (A diastolic fall of 10 mmHg or more is part of the international consensus definition — international.)

NICE NG136 [1]: aged under 80, clinic below 140/90 and ABPM/HBPM below 135/85. Consider ABPM or HBPM alongside clinic readings where white-coat effect or masked hypertension is suspected. People who monitor at home should be given training and advice.
Amlodipine is long-acting (BNF); extra doses for a high reading do not act quickly and add to ankle swelling and postural symptoms. Change treatment only on a valid average.

NICE NG136 [1]: clinic BP ≥180/120 with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, AKI), needs same-day specialist referral. A single home 178/100 with no symptoms is not an emergency.
Worry and repeated checking raise readings. A fixed schedule, not checking when anxious, and addressing the health anxiety are part of management.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you interpret data before acting on it. It is failed by chasing the highest number, by ignoring technique, and by brushing off the anxiety that drives the readings.

items.why: Changing treatment on unreliable readings is unsafe and may cause postural hypotension.
items.fix: Standardise first, then decide on the average.

items.fail: Never asking how she takes the readings.
items.why: Technique and timing explain most variability.
items.fix: Ask when, where and how; teach the NG136 HBPM routine.

items.fail: No pulse check or thought of AF.
items.why: NG136 requires a pulse check before automated measurement; AF makes readings erratic and changes management.
items.fix: Manual pulse, manual BP if irregular, ECG.

items.why: Low readings may reflect postural hypotension or over-treatment.
items.fix: Ask about postural symptoms; sitting and standing BP.

items.why: Dismissive labelling damages trust and misses the chance to break the loop.
items.fix: Explain how worry raises readings and agree a checking boundary.

items.why: Without it she will keep reacting to every number.
items.fix: Name the symptoms that need 999 or same-day contact; everything else waits for review.
